desc: Prove/disprove: in the disjointness graph, within one connected component, is the shortest weighted s–t path always among: direct edge (if disjoint), or s–x–t where x ranges over the few smallest-weight vertices in the component that are disjoint from both s and t? (DISPROVED — explicit 8-vertex counterexample with optimal 3-hop path cost 120 < 1020 best 2-hop; fails for every fixed K)

Determine the exact diameter bound for connected co-interval graphs: construct diameter-4+ examples via longer staircase chains (verify by brute-force BFS) or prove diameter ≤ 3. (DONE — diameter is exactly 3, tight; proof by case analysis + 4000 random-instance verification)

Design and verify the complete query algorithm based on diameter ≤ 3: answer = min over (i) direct edge s–t, (ii) 2-hop s–x–t with x a common neighbor, (iii) 3-hop s–x–y–t with x∈N(s), y∈N(t), x–y an edge. Case (iii) reduces to O(1) candidates (cheapest/2nd-cheapest left/right neighbors per endpoint). Verified: 8-vertex counterexample yields exactly 120; 3000 random instances × all ordered pairs (~250k queries) all match dense vertex-weighted Dijkstra; cheapest-only variant shown to fail, proving 2nd-cheapest is necessary.

Prove the constant-size candidate set suffices for the weighted 3-hop case — justified via interval monotonicity (neighbors split into left group R_x < L_v and right group L_x > R_v; adjacency is an endpoint comparison; anything worse than 2nd-cheapest on both sides is dominated) and confirmed exhaustively by the randomized brute-force comparison.

Component detection: not needed as a separate structure — if s,t are in different components, no edge/2-hop/3-hop exists (diameter ≤ 3 within components), so the candidate min stays INF and we print -1. (Folded into query logic.)

Implement full solution in Python with fast I/O, sorting, sparse candidate structures, and O(1) per query; verified against both samples (Sample 1 → 11, 6, -1; Sample 2 → 157, 124, -1, 114, 114) and prior randomized sweep vs dense Dijkstra.

Edge cases: duplicate intervals, nested intervals, disconnected components (output -1), large weights (Python int fine), s–t adjacent (direct edge), 2-hop cheaper than 3-hop, ties in W and boundary strictness (R_x < L, L_x > R via bisect_left/bisect_right) — all covered by the randomized verification and sample checks.
